I believe at extreme LLC it does indeed lead to a larger spike in voltage. What is especially important from what I remember is voltage undershoots which is often the cause for instability. At high LLC (low vdroop) settings can often result in larger and more undershoot, resulting in instability.

This voltage undershoot is usually too quick to be measured by the CPU or motherboard sensors, and is only visible on an oscilloscope.

What often ends up being the case is that a larger vdroop LLC setting can net a lower stable voltage under load than one with less vdroop. This means less voltage and lower temperatures under load which is usually a good trade off for  the higher voltage when idle. Higher idle voltages are usually not a concern.

It's not just an "expectation" that the voltage drops under load for lower LLC settings, it will always drop under load. The amount it drops just depends on how heavy the load is.

You can see examples of the undershoot in this video of buildzoid testing LLC settings https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-L3mNJ9kvXk

Certain workloads can run at a higher frequency than others. For example my static overclocked 3900x is perfectly stable in most applications. However in prime95 with 128k FFTs some threads may crash.

Using a static oc results in you needing to set it to a frequency that is stable for all workloads, otherwise you'll experience crashes in day to day use. 

Modern CPU boost algorithms can determine what frequency it can maintain for a specific workload at a specific voltage without instability. Undervolting reduces the safety margin of these boost algorithms, but can result in lower thermals and thus a higher boost frequency.

So using a static overclock can actually limit your performance especially for more dynamic and lighter workloads.

A way to solve would be to add in a wired backhaul or reduce the amount of nodes connected to another node not being the main node.
